# Frozen source instructions — Debate 287

Motion, byte-identical: **Does God exist?** Adam Lloyd Johnson is pro, “God exists”; Dan Barker is con, “God’s existence is unproven”. This is the March 5, 2022 FREEFLO formal debate, uploaded March 25. The original event year remains 2022; website assessment date is the actual rendering date.

## Complete source and retained scope

Read the entire indexed transcript (2651 zero-based canonical events) for context and exclusion boundaries. Only these substantive formal speeches are eligible: Johnson opening 299–675, Barker opening 688–1131, Barker rebuttal 1179–1486, Johnson rebuttal 1491–1743, Barker closing 2274–2380, Johnson closing 2382–2476. Logistics between retained speeches are unscored. No formal cross-examination occurs. The assessed envelope is 628079–5403320 ms; the entire 3835559–4948000 ms Q&A/transition interval is excluded. Event 2273 is mixed transition and excluded in full. Everything before event 299 and after event 2476 is also unscored. Canonical caption display times sometimes overlap; use substantive word ownership and do not select a span crossing an excluded interval.

Both formal openings, both rebuttals and both complete closings are present. Gaps after events 298 and 1488 are setup/handoff silence, not missing arguments. Canonical captions, not independent audio, supply the source. No direct listening or independent transcript corroboration is claimed. The original English public media endpoint denied audio acquisition with HTTP 403; no paid call occurred.

## Scope-dependent inferences prohibited

No credit, penalty, concession, response link, quotation or absence inference may come from audience questions, either debater’s Q&A answers, their dependent replies, or the hosts’ pre/post discussion. A closing’s independently restated claim is eligible, but “as we discussed” does not import excluded support.

Barker’s Q&A distinction between believing a god exists and worshipping/accepting that god is excluded. Do not use that answer to prove Johnson’s formal reported attribution false; assess the formal claim only against retained evidence, including Barker’s formal openness to belief. Johnson’s Q&A reply on omniscience and free will is excluded: neither response credit nor an assertion that he never answered in the whole event is allowed. The source scope can support only observations about development in the formal rounds. Barker’s postclosing praise of the multiverse rebuttal and Johnson’s later acknowledgement of harm-based moral knowledge are excluded; neither counts as concession.

## Preserve burdens and qualifications

Johnson advances a cumulative best-explanation case from the universe’s beginning, fine-tuning and objective moral truths; he expressly treats the motion as mere theism rather than proving Christianity or the Bible. The rebuttal briefly proposes the Trinity as moral grounding, but do not expand the frozen motion. His educated-believer remarks expressly deny that smart believers themselves prove God. His moral argument concerns the existence/grounding of objective moral truths, not whether atheists can behave well or know right from wrong. Preserve his conceded limits of certainty and explanatory inference.

Barker’s stated standard is insufficient evidence and reasonable doubt, not a burden to disprove every possible god. His FANG objection is the free-will argument for the non-existence of God: he argues that an omniscient being knows its own future and therefore lacks the period of uncertainty he says free choice requires; preserve his acknowledgement that other god definitions may escape that argument. He distinguishes mind-dependent moral values from objective assessment of consequences; do not replace his harm-based proposal with “anything goes”. He says objections give justifiable nonbelief rather than strict proof. The problem of evil is mentioned but not substantively developed; do not invent a detailed evil argument or impose an obligation to cover every possible route.

## Recognition uncertainty — mandatory restrictions

Keep every caption word unchanged in source excerpts. Do not silently fix names, references, technical words or negations. Never count automatic-recognition uncertainty as a speaker’s error. Slides are not captured: do not invent their particular numerical constants, lists or citations. Robert Audi, Koons, Stenger and Stavrakopoulou are recognized imperfectly; names alone cannot support a penalty or exact featured quote.

Events 1274–1313 contain the firing-squad story and possibly corrupted numerator/denominator wording. Do not quote or score the literal number of shots/prisoners, “none of them missed,” or the ratio idiom. Do not invent a corrected numerical argument. Barker’s surrounding explicit argument that varying multiple constants can permit other life, that a multiverse is an alternative hypothesis, and that observers must occupy a life-permitting universe remains eligible on its unambiguous words. Neither numerical competence nor numerical incompetence may be inferred from this passage.

Events 1595–1597 appear to drop a negation in Johnson’s statement about immaterial things. Events 1608–1613 may confuse material/immaterial in his attribution to philosophers. Events 1629–1631 may again misrecognize immaterial. Do not penalize apparent contradiction, claim that Johnson denies immaterial reality, adjudicate named philosophers’ positions, or quote any corrupted clause. Johnson’s explicit surrounding claims that abstract objects exist outside space/time and that an immaterial mind causes physical effects remain eligible as stated; do not silently correct the caption. Do not select a corrupted fragment as the sole warrant for a move.

These restrictions do not authorize omission of a load-bearing argument or manufacturing high confidence. Select its smallest complete unambiguous source passage where available; if material ownership or content still depends on uncertain words, flag it below high with the required verification reason and notify the controller. Audio verification remains mandatory for below-high selected moves before adjudication.

## Featured quotations and selection

Each side must have at least one exact 3–18 word excerpt expressing a complete thought, with meaning-changing qualifications retained. Choose another complete excerpt if a qualification cannot fit. No clipped predicate, invented completion, recognition-corrupted text, imported opponent commitment or excluded source is eligible. Complete short candidates exist in the formal moral-grounding case and Barker’s qualified nonbelief conclusion. Selection, structure, burden mapping and importance remain the inventory reviewer’s score-blind decisions; no target counts, ratings or winner are prescribed.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson

moves.warrant: Johnson proposes abductive reasoning that compares possible explanations for an observed effect.
moves.inference: The causal argument is presented as an inference to the best explanation rather than a deductive identification of God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage begins with Johnson’s distinction between a cause and God and ends after he defines the abductive method he will use.
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is part of Johnson’s uninterrupted opening.

sourceSpan.excerpt: now you might notice with this argument a lot of people notice i thought this was an argument for god it doesn't end with god it just ends with a cause why do people think this cause is god well many thinkers have concluded that this the best explanation for this cause is some sort of a supreme being through abductive reasoning through reasoning like an inference to the best explanation similarly that's how we often think through things a lot of possibilities some effect that we see something happen we think through there's all sorts of possibilities of what that could be but what's the best explanation of it that's the abductive reasoning that i'll be using

moves.description: Johnson distinguishes a generic cause from God and proposes abductive comparison among possible explanations, intending to identify a supreme being as the universe’s best explanation.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson candidly distinguishes the syllogism’s generic cause from God and identifies the further step as abductive reasoning, an inference comparing possible explanations rather than claiming deductive certainty. Principal limitation: This move supplies no criteria or developed comparison showing why a supreme being outranks rival candidate causes, because the substantive evidence is deferred to later arguments. Live burden: Johnson must complete the announced best-explanation comparison and show that the proposed supreme being explains the observed effect better than live alternatives; the method therefore announces a necessary comparison successfully without yet performing the comparison on which its preferred explanation depends.

moves.description: Barker distinguishes ordinary atheistic nonbelief from hard denial, inferring that his burden is to assess Johnson’s case rather than disprove every possible god.

Principal limitation: The move is chiefly definitional, and Barker’s broader suggestion about how most atheists use the label receives only light support beyond his own stated position. Live burden: Barker must critically assess whether Johnson’s affirmative case warrants belief while preserving his declared openness, rather than substituting a positive proof of universal nonexistence; this disciplined scope is especially important because Barker’s position remains compatible with being persuaded by an adequate affirmative case.

Live burden: Johnson must defend the strength of those three effects and their proposed best explanations, because distinguishing a wish for more evidence from a denial of all credible evidence does not establish that the available cumulative evidence is sufficiently compelling to defeat Barker’s stated reasonable doubt.

moves.description: Barker assigns the theist a demanding proof burden and argues that reasonable doubt warrants withholding belief until the existence of God is established beyond that threshold.

Principal limitation: The analogy does not justify importing “beyond reasonable doubt” as the governing standard for a philosophical best-explanation dispute, and that threshold may demand more than the motion requires. Live burden: Barker must evaluate the affirmative evidence under a defensible standard while showing why residual doubt is reasonable, not invoke admitted uncertainty as sufficient defeat; the standard remains underspecified even though Barker distinguishes failure of proof from a proof that God is impossible.

moves.description: Johnson combines cosmological, fine-tuning, and moral considerations, arguing that their convergence and shared fit make God the best overall explanation of reality.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson clearly synthesizes the beginning, design, and moral routes, acknowledges arguments against God and the absence of absolute certainty, and reaches a proportionate most-reasonable-explanation conclusion. Principal limitation: Combining three abductive lines does not repair unresolved weaknesses inside their causal, design, and grounding bridges, and the closing adds little systematic comparison beyond the earlier warrants. Live burden: Johnson must show how the lines jointly outweigh their live defects and rival explanations rather than relying on breadth alone to establish cumulative superiority; the closing succeeds as synthesis and calibration even though it cannot supply missing evidence for each component merely by restating them together.

moves.description: Barker argues that publicly accessible evidence for God remains inadequate and cannot distinguish religious conviction from alternatives, so withholding belief is the responsible inference.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Barker directly raises the public-evidence burden, distinguishes familiar cultural stories from stronger evidence, and repeatedly limits his conclusion to reasonable nonbelief rather than claiming that evidential absence disproves God. Principal limitation: Continued debate and lack of scientific recognition do not establish the absence claimed, and the move largely precedes systematic engagement with Johnson’s three specific arguments. Live burden: Barker must assess the actual causal, design, and moral evidence rather than rely on “hiding,” debate, or recognition as rough proxies for its quality; the rhetoric about puny evidence also gives Johnson’s proposed explanatory evidence less charitable treatment than Barker’s qualified conclusion otherwise suggests.

moves.description: Barker says Johnson has not connected the required evidential steps, remains unconvinced but open to persuasion, and concludes that qualified nonbelief is still justified.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Barker returns to his motion-level burden, asks whether the stated evidential absences were filled, and carefully distinguishes remaining unconvinced from claiming disproof while expressly leaving himself open to persuasion. Principal limitation: Personal nonconviction is not independent evidence, and the closing compresses its verdict without restating the specific defects or systematically weighing Johnson’s cumulative case. Live burden: Barker must rely on the previously developed objections to show why the affirmative bridges remain insufficient, not treat his continuing psychological state as their demonstration; Barker also correctly notes that evil was not developed here, avoiding both invented argument and an improper penalty for that omission.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: The universe had a beginning and therefore had a cause.
moves.warrant: Whatever has a beginning must have a cause, and the universe had a beginning.
moves.inference: A cause of the universe is required.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the smallest contiguous passage containing both premises and the stated conclusion of Johnson’s first-cause argument.

moves.attributionRationale: The passage falls within Johnson’s uninterrupted opening after his named handoff.
moves.importanceRationale: This is one of the three principal constructive lines in the cumulative case.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the causal premise for moving from cosmic beginning to a transcendent explanation.

sourceSpan.excerpt: the first argument that i'm going to cover is a contemporary version of the first cause argument so here it goes just a nutshell basic version of it premise one whatever has a beginning must have a cause premise two the universe had a beginning therefore the universe had a cause

moves.description: Johnson argues that whatever begins to exist has a cause and that the universe began to exist, inferring only that the universe had a generic cause.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: The explicit two-premise syllogism cleanly separates the claimed beginning, the causal maxim, and the limited conclusion that the universe requires a cause, making Johnson’s cosmic-origin reasoning unusually easy to audit. Principal limitation: Neither the universe’s beginning nor the unrestricted claim that whatever begins must have a cause receives scientific or independent metaphysical support in this condensed presentation. Live burden: Johnson still must defend both premises and explain why ordinary causal expectations apply to the universe’s beginning before this generic cause can support God; the missing support matters because both premises carry the entire inferential load before any divine attributes enter the case.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Describing a cause as prior to time treats time as though it could exist outside itself.
moves.warrant: Barker says time is a dimension and compares asking what is prior to time with asking what is higher than height or broader than width.
moves.inference: The proposed temporal relation between the universe and its cause is not coherently stated.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact passage contains Barker’s complete prior-to-time objection and its dimensional analogies.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: how can you describe prior to time
moves.attributionRationale: The objection appears in Barker’s uninterrupted opening and contains clear wording with no noted recognition uncertainty.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly challenges the causal-to-divine bridge’s use of a cause existing before time.

burdenContact.rationale: It tests whether the claimed relation between a timeless cause and temporal beginning is coherent.

responseComponents.description: Challenges Johnson’s inference that the universe’s cause existed prior to time.

sourceSpan.excerpt: talking admitting that space and time came into existence at the big bang and you get saying what something must have come prior how can you describe prior to time time is a dimension you know what is what is higher than height what is broader than width it's a dimension that we're talking about and yet adam seems to be talking about them as if they were things as if the as if time somehow could exist outside of time which is not a coherent concept

moves.description: Barker treats time as a dimension and compares “prior to time” with “higher than height,” inferring that Johnson’s proposed temporal relation is incoherent.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Barker’s comparison of “prior to time” with “higher than height” and “broader than width” identifies the category problem in using temporal language where time itself is said to begin. Principal limitation: The dimensional analogy challenges Johnson’s wording but does not rule out a nontemporal explanatory or causal relation, an alternative the move does not consider. Live burden: Barker must show that the required dependence is incoherent even without an earlier temporal event, rather than defeating only the vocabulary of priority; his argument targets Johnson’s formulation without establishing the much broader conclusion that every conceivable atemporal explanatory relation is logically impossible.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: The cause of the universe is reasonably characterized as spaceless, timeless, immaterial, and powerful.
moves.warrant: Johnson says the universe consists of space, time, and matter, so a cause preceding their beginning would not itself be spatial, temporal, or material; causing a universe also indicates power.
moves.inference: The first cause has attributes associated with a supreme being.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This immediately follows the causal syllogism and contains Johnson’s complete causal-to-divine attribute bridge.
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is in Johnson’s uninterrupted opening and uses clear wording outside the later recognition-caution ranges.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the necessary bridge from a generic cause to the kind of cause relevant to the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies the properties Johnson infers from causing space, time, and matter.

sourceSpan.excerpt: since the universe itself the universe just is space time and matter then those things didn't exist until the universe began therefore it's reasonable to conclude that this cause which existed prior to space-time and matter is spaceless timeless and immaterial also i think it's reasonable to conclude this cause is very powerful since he brought the universe into existence

moves.description: Johnson infers that the cause of spacetime and matter cannot itself be spatial, temporal, or material, intending this transcendence to narrow the explanation toward God.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson gives a definite bridge from a generic cause toward the motion by connecting the beginning of space, time, and matter with spacelessness, timelessness, immateriality, and causal power. Principal limitation: The compressed account does not establish that a cause cannot share or originate with those categories, and “prior to time” risks importing the temporal relation it denies. Live burden: Johnson must clarify a nontemporal causal relation and supply more than the bare act of causing a universe to justify the further attribution of power; the move also leaves unclear whether creating those dimensions entails lacking them rather than standing in some other relation.

moves.warrant: Barker argues that experience supplies no example of things that do not begin to exist against which beginning things can be contrasted.

moves.description: Barker argues that Johnson’s causal premise divides reality into beginning and nonbeginning things without observed examples of the latter, allegedly importing its conclusion.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Barker tests Johnson’s causal premise by asking how reality can be divided into beginning and nonbeginning classes when experience supplies no example of the latter. Principal limitation: The conditional claim that whatever begins has a cause does not assert that an unbegun thing exists, so the stated question-begging diagnosis mistakes a category condition for its members. Live burden: Barker must challenge the causal premise with relevant warrant or counterexample rather than treating the absence of experienced nonbeginning things as proof that Johnson imported God; the two-class formulation is useful because it exposes where Barker thinks the universal causal rule lacks experiential support.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Calling a timeless and spaceless cause powerful imports a physical concept that requires work over time.
moves.warrant: Barker defines power as work over time and asks how an entity outside space and time could possess it.
moves.inference: The cosmological conclusion does not coherently supply the divine attribute of power.

moves.attributionRationale: This is within Barker’s independently introduced formal closing after the excluded interval.

burdenContact.rationale: It tests whether a stated divine attribute is meaningful under the proposed timeless definition.

sourceSpan.excerpt: you you mentioned uh the prime mover uh you said this prime mover or whatever you call it the cause outside of the big bang or whatever you however the words you use it you said this being has to be incredibly powerful you said but power is work over time power is a physical natural thing how can an immaterial being who doesn't exist in space or time how can it have power what would power even mean to a being you only would say he's all-powerful if you're comparing it to something else like he created a puny universe that way you can't say look how powerful i am it doesn't mean anything at all so you're you're you're smuggling concepts into your premises that don't belong there and it's it amounts almost amounts to begging the question and again i i do think

moves.description: Barker argues that power means work performed through time and physical change, intending to show that a timeless, spaceless powerful being is conceptually empty.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Barker isolates Johnson’s attribution of power and states a challenge: physical power is work over time, so that definition conflicts with a cause outside time. Principal limitation: Treating the physics quantity as exhaustive equivocates between measurable physical power and causal capacity, leaving the claim that a cause can produce an effect untouched. Live burden: Barker must show that Johnson’s intended sense of causal power is incoherent, rather than assuming without warrant that every possible meaning must involve physical work over time; the physical formula establishes one legitimate sense of power but does not prove that Johnson used that sense in his causal conclusion.
